question.text: This city that sits on both sides of the Dnieper ("duh-NEE-per") River is home to the St. Sophia Cathedral and the historic Golden Gate. It is the capital of the Ukraine.
question.clue: It's not Novgorod, but a grand prince of this city was named Yaroslav the Wise.

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about leaders with titles in common.
swap.text: Give the title last held by Nicholas II of Russia before he was killed in 1918.
swap.clue: It's not in Germany, but one holder of this title issued the Anti-Semitic May Laws, which prohibited the creation of new towns by Jews.

question.text: Prior to the Bolshevik Revolution, Russia was briefly ruled by the Provisional government under this man, whose disastrous June Offensive led in part to the Bolshevik rise.
question.clue: He came to prominence for his role in exposing the spy Roman Malinovsky and later pushed agendas of universal suffrage and increased freedom of speech after being named Minister of Justice.

swap.leadin: In 1978, Georgi Markov died after a ricin-filled pellet was injected into his thigh, probably by an umbrella gun.
swap.text: The pellet was allegedly designed by this security agency, led at the time by Yuri Andropov.
swap.clue: It evolved from earlier organizations, such as Cheka, but came directly from the NKVD, which had been led by Levrenty Beria.

question.leadin: Russia was feeling really revolutionary in the early 20th century.
question.text: Name this last Emperor of Russia, an unpopular Romanov who was responsible for a massacre of protesters on Bloody Sunday and abdicated after the February Revolution of 1917.
question.clue: Most of this ruler's fleet was lost in the Battle of Tsushima in a war that ended as a humiliating loss to Japan.

swap.text: Nikita Khrushchev had a notable shoe-banging incident at a UN meeting. Not long before, this speech of his was given to the leadership of the Communist Party and denounced the deceased Stalin's personality cult.
swap.answerHtml: The Secret Speech (or “On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences”)
swap.clue: It repudiated Zhdanovism and was partially responsible for riots and demonstrations in Georgia.

question.text: This sucessor to Khrushchev governed the Soviet Republic during the Era of Stagnation and signed the SALT treaties with Gerald Ford.
question.clue: His economic policies have been described as "the lowest stage of socialism," and this man is remembered for recognizing postwar European boundaries with the Helsinki Accords.

swap.text: Novgorodian pirates known as Ushkuyniks plied this long Russian river, attacking cities on it such as Kazan and Astrakhan. This river was the main conduit of trade between the Rus and Sassanid Persia.
swap.clue: Flowing through Nizhniy Novgorod and Samara, this river's canal to the Don provides the most direct connection between the Sea of Azov (AH-soff) and the world's largest lake.

question.text: He married Zoe Paleologus, the niece of Constantine XI, and ordered Vladimir Gusev to compile his legal reforms in the Sudebnik. He also ended the tribute to Khan Ahmed and won a major victory at Ugra. For 15 points, name this son of Vasily II, the first man to claim the title "Grand Duke of all Russians" and namesake of a vicious grandson.
question.answerHtml: Ivan III of Russia [or Ivan the Great; or Ivan III Vasilevich]
question.clue: The Great Stand on the Ugra took place following this ruler's refusal to pay tribute to Akhmat Khan, a move symbolizing the end of the Tatar yoke on Moscow.

swap.leadin: In addition to the ball drop in Times Square, the New Year often sees regime change. For the stated points-.
swap.text: For 10 points, on December 31, 1999, this first president of the Russian Federation resigned.
swap.clue: According to one story, this politician drunkenly wandered outside the White House in his underwear looking for pizza.

question.leadin: She has been called "the German woman on the Czar's throne"
question.text: Name this empress of Russia who reigned from 1762 to 1796. Like Frederick II of Prussia and Joseph II of Austria, she was referred to as an "Enlightened Despot" and corresponded with philosophes like Voltaire and Diderot.
question.answerHtml: Catherine II [or Catherine the Great or Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst or Yekaterina Velikaya or Yekaterina Alekseyevna; prompt on “Catherine”]
question.clue: This ruler took power in a coup against her husband Peter III.

swap.text: The Russians under Alexander Menshikov won this 1709 battle near the namesake Ukrainian city. Fleeing Swedish troops under Adam Lewenhaupt surrendered at Perevolochna shortly after this battle.
swap.clue: The siege precipitating it was the first phase of one side's plan to strike at the other's capital, a plan that was bolstered by the defection of Ivan Mazepa.

question.leadin: Answer the following about Soviet historiography.
question.text: Soviet textbooks blamed the Nazis for this 1940 massacre of Polish soldiers and intelligentsia, though it was actually perpetrated by the NKVD under Lavrenty Beria.
question.clue: The Soviet secret police carried out this 1940 massacre of Polish nationals in the namesake Russian woodlands. About 22,000 were slain during it, and the Soviets blamed it on the Nazis.

swap.leadin: In principle, any resident of this city could ring a bell to summon its entire population to either its "Trade" or "Sophia" sides.
swap.text: Name this mercantile city-state that housed the easternmost kontor of the Hanseatic League. This city's conquest by Muscovy after the 1471 Battle of Shelon led to the abolition of its veche ("VETCH-yeh") assembly.
swap.answerHtml: Veliky Novgorod [or Novgorod Republic or Lord Novgorod the Great; reject “Nizhny Novgorod”]
swap.clue: This city's St. Sophia Cathedral is home to the bones of Yaroslav the Wise.

question.text: This oral historian wrote Secondhand Time and interviewed various firefighters and "liquidators" tasked with limiting the damage of a nuclear disaster near Pripyat.

swap.leadin: Name the following battles of the Crimean War FTPE.
swap.text: John Pettyjohns and Henry Percy were among the twelve soldiers award the Victoria Cross for their action in this November fifth, 1854 battle; a Russian loss which served to divert strength from the Siege of Sevastopol.
swap.clue: As was a theme for the larger war, poor British leadership, this time under by Lord Raglan, was partially ameliorated by English bravery.

question.text: The leader of the pro-German government, Pavlo Skoropadskyi, revived the use of this title while leading Ukraine in 1918. This title was traditionally used by leaders of a sich until abolished by Catherine the Great.
question.clue: Holders of this title, who carried a gem-encrusted mace called a bulawa ("boo-WAH-va"), were elected by the Sich ("seetch") Rada.

swap.text: After the death of Feodor III, the Miloslavsky family incited this group of guardsmen to riot against the Naryshkins and other political leaders. One of their leaders was Ivan Khovansky.
swap.clue: This unit, which was often accompanied by horsemen whose name translates to "Boyar's Children," were gradually incorporated into the normal army by Peter the Great.

question.leadin: This war was touched off when troops under Jacob de la Gardie captured a fortress at Ladoga.
question.text: Name this 1610 to 1617 war between Russia and Sweden, which ended with Sweden receiving large territorial gains in the Treaty of Stolbovo.
question.clue: This war, launched by Gustavus Adolphus on the fledgling state of Mikhail Romanov, was justified by Russia's refusal to hand over Novgorod to the forces of Jacob de la Gardie. It forced the Treaty of Stolbovo, which cut off Russian Baltic access and stretched Swedish territory to Lake Ladoga and Lake Peipus, leading to the high point of Swedish power.

swap.text: The "green army" is the name sometimes given to Aleksandr Antonov's forces during this rebellion. This peasant rebellion took place during the Russian Civil War and was ended by Mikhail Tukhachevsky.
swap.clue: This rebellion, which was suppressed with a force of one hundred thousand Red Army troops under Mikhail Tukhachevsky, who used tactics like firing poisonous gas at peasant strongholds.
